extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical geometry (Euclid), mathematics instructors and researchers interested in Euclidean proportion and similarity
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from Euclid (Books V–VI) giving definitions and theorems about proportion, compound ratios, and similarity of plane figures, with proofs and corollaries. Useful as canonical statements and proof sketches of classical proportion/similarity results.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XIX. THEOR.
rubrics_metrics.description: If a whole magnitude be to a whole, as a magnitude taken from the first is to a magnitude taken from the other; the remainder shall be to the remainder, as the whole to the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement: Let AB be to CD as AE (a magnitude taken from AB) is to CF (a magnitude taken from CD); then remainder EB is to remainder FD as whole AB to whole CD. Proof uses alternation and previous proportion propositions (inversion/composition): AB:CD :: AE:CF implies BA:AE :: DC:CF, and by properties of proportions when magnitudes taken jointly are proportional they remain so separately, yielding BE:DF :: AB:CD.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary to PROP. XIX
rubrics_metrics.description: If the whole be to the whole, as a magnitude taken from the first is to a magnitude taken from the other; the remainder likewise is to the remainder, as the magnitude taken from the first to that taken from the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows directly from the proposition by applying the same alternation/composition reasoning to the corresponding parts; the demonstration is contained in the preceding proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. E. THEOR. (Conversion of proportion)
rubrics_metrics.description: If four magnitudes be proportionals, they are also proportionals by conversion, that is, the first is to its excess above the second, as the third to its excess above the fourth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement: If AB:BE :: CD:DF then BA:AE :: DC:CF. Proof sketch: use division to form AE:EB :: CF:FD, then inversion to get BE:EA :: DF:FC, and composition to obtain BA:AE :: DC:CF. The proposition is proved by applying division, inversion and composition of ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XX. THEOR.
rubrics_metrics.description: If there be three magnitudes, and other three, which, taken two and two, have the same ratio; if the first be greater than the third, the fourth shall be greater than the sixth; and if equal, equal; and if less, less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let A,B,C and D,E,F be such that A:B :: D:E and B:C :: E:F. Proof: compare ratios to a common magnitude B and use that a greater magnitude has a greater ratio to the same magnitude; deduce D has a greater (or equal/less) ratio to E than F does, hence D>F (or equal/less). The proof proceeds by cases (greater, equal, less).

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXI. THEOR. (Cross-ordered three)
rubrics_metrics.description: If there be three magnitudes, and other three, which have the same ratio taken two and two, but in a cross order; if the first magnitude be greater than the third, the fourth shall be greater than the sixth; and if equal, equal; and if less, less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-order means e.g. A:B :: E:F and B:C :: D:E. Proof parallels Prop. XX: compare ratios to a common magnitude and apply inversion and previous results to derive the corresponding inequality/equality relationships between D and F; the argument handles greater/equal/less cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXII. THEOR. (Ex aequali: chained ratios in order)
rubrics_metrics.description: If there be any number of magnitudes, and as many others, which, taken two and two in order, have the same ratio; the first shall have to the last of the first magnitudes the same ratio which the first of the others has to the last.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also cited as ex aequali or ex aequo. Proof constructs equimultiples of corresponding magnitudes and applies Prop. XX (about three) repeatedly: if A:B :: D:E and B:C :: E:F then A:C :: D:F, and similarly for any number of magnitudes by composing ratios via equimultiples.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXIII. THEOR. (Ex aequali in cross order)
rubrics_metrics.description: If there be any number of magnitudes, and as many others, which, taken two and two in a cross order, have the same ratio, the first shall have to the last of the first magnitudes the same ratio which the first of the others has to the last.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also cited as ex aequali in proportione perturbata or ex aequo perturbate. Proof: take equimultiples of the magnitudes to reduce to the three-magnitude cross-order case (Prop. XXI) and then extend by induction to arbitrarily many magnitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXIV. THEOR.
rubrics_metrics.description: If the first has to the second the same ratio which the third has to the fourth; and the fifth to the second the same ratio which the sixth has to the fourth; the first and fifth together shall have to the second the same ratio which the third and sixth together have to the fourth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let AB:C :: DE:F and BG:C :: EH:F; then AG:C :: DH:F. Proof uses inversion and ex aequali to combine ratios and then composition of proportional magnitudes to obtain the ratio of sums. Proposition includes demonstration and is followed by corollaries obtained by using division instead of composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 1 to PROP. XXIV
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the same hypothesis, the excess of the first and fifth shall be to the second as the excess of the third and sixth to the fourth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstration is same as the proposition but with division used instead of composition (i.e., applies to differences/excesses rather than sums).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 2 to PROP. XXIV
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposition holds true of two ranks of magnitudes, whatever be their number, of which each of the first rank has to the second magnitude the same ratio that the corresponding one of the second rank has to a fourth magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalization remark: the same reasoning extends to arrays (two ranks) of magnitudes paired by equal ratios; proof is evident from the main proposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. XXV. THEOR.
rubrics_metrics.description: If four magnitudes of the same kind are proportionals, the greatest and least of them together are greater than the other two together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let AB, CD, E, F be proportional with AB greatest and F least; then AB+F > CD+E. Proof: take AG = E and CH = F, use proportionality to get AB:CD :: AG:CH, then compare remainders and add equal magnitudes to obtain the inequality. Uses previous results about remainders and composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. F. THEOR. (Compound ratios equality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ratios which are compounded of the same ratios, are the same with one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If A:B :: D:E and B:C :: E:F then the compound ratio A:C (compound of A:B and B:C) is the same as D:F (compound of D:E and E:F). Proof by reducing to three magnitudes and applying ex aequali (Prop. XXII) and definitions of compound ratio; extends by induction to any number of factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. G. THEOR.
rubrics_metrics.description: If several ratios be the same with several ratios, each to each; the ratio which is compounded of ratios which are the same with the first ratios, each to each, is the same with the ratio compounded of ratios which are the same with the other ratios, each to each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given pairs A:B :: E:F and C:D :: G:H and alternatives K:L :: A:B, L:M :: C:D, show compound K:M :: N:P (constructed similarly) equals N:P (compound of E:F and G:H). Proof applies ex aequali and definition of compound ratio to translate equalities across corresponding factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. H. THEOR.
rubrics_metrics.description: If a ratio compounded of several ratios be the same with a ratio compounded of any other ratios, and if one of the first ratios, or a ratio compounded of any of the first, be the same with one of the last ratios, or with the ratio compounded of any of the last; then the ratio compounded of the remaining ratios of the first is the same with the ratio compounded of those remaining of the last.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement describes cancellation in compound ratios: if product of many ratios equals product of many others, and if a subproduct from one equals a subproduct from the other, then removing those equal subproducts yields equality of the remaining compound ratios. Proof uses inversion and ex aequali to rearrange and cancel corresponding compounded portions.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. K. THEOR. (General cancellation in compound ratios)
rubrics_metrics.description: If there be any number of ratios, and any number of other ratios such that the ratio compounded of ratios which are the same with the first ratios, each to each, is the same with the ratio compounded of ratios which are the same with the last ratios; and if one of the first ratios, or the ratio which is compounded of ratios which are the same with several of the first ratios, each to each, be the same with one of the last ratios, or with the ratio compounded of ratios which are the same, each to each, with several of the last ratios: then the ratio compounded of ratios which are the same with the remaining ratios of the first, each to each, is the same with the ratio compounded of ratios which are the same with those remaining of the last, each to each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A further generalization of Prop. H to arbitrarily many factors (chains of ratios). The proof constructs representative magnitudes (S,T,V,X,... and Y,Z,a,...), maps corresponding equalities, and applies the same ex aequali/inversion reasoning to deduce equality of the remaining compounded ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition I (Book VI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar rectilineal figures are those which have their several angles equal, each to each, and the sides about the equal angles proportionals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition: similarity requires equality of corresponding angles and proportionality of corresponding sides around those equal angles. This is the classical Euclidean notion of similar plane figures used throughout Book VI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition II (Book VI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal figures, viz. triangles and parallelograms, are such as have their sides about two of their angles proportionals in such manner, that a side of the first figure is to a side of the other, as the remaining side of this other is to the remaining side of the first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines a particular relation between two figures (reciprocal) used in later propositions; the sides around two angles are proportionally paired so that cross-side proportionalities hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition III (Book VI)
rubrics_metrics.description: A straight line is said to be cut in extreme and mean ratio, when the whole is to the greater segment, as the greater segment is to the less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the classical extreme and mean (golden-section) ratio property for a line divided into two segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition IV (Book VI)
rubrics_metrics.description: The altitude of any figure is the straight line drawn from its vertex perpendicular to the base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard geometric definition of altitude used in statements comparing areas and proportions of triangles and parallelograms.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. I. (Book VI) THEOR.
rubrics_metrics.description: Triangles and parallelograms of the same altitude are one to another as their bases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If triangles ABC and ACD and parallelograms EC and CF have the same altitude (perpendicular from A to BD), then triangle ABC : triangle ACD = base BC : base CD, and parallelogram EC : CF = BC : CD. Proof: cover bases by equal-numbered copies (equimultiples) and use equality/comparison of triangles with equal altitudes; parallelogram results follow because parallelograms are doubles of triangles and equimultiple reasoning carries over.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary to PROP. I
rubrics_metrics.description: Triangles and parallelograms that have equal altitudes are one to another as their bases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placed figures with bases on same line and drawn perpendiculars from vertices; since altitudes equal and bases are comparable, the same ratio-of-bases relation between figures holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. II. (Book VI) THEOR.
rubrics_metrics.description: If a straight line be drawn parallel to one of the sides of a triangle, it shall cut the other sides, or those produced, proportionally: and if the sides, or the sides produced, be cut proportionally, the straight line which joins the points of section shall be parallel to the remaining side of the triangle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forward: If DE is parallel to BC in triangle ABC, then BD:DA = CE:EA. Proof uses equal triangles on same base between parallels, and equality of ratios of triangles with same altitude. Converse: given BD:DA = CE:EA, show DE is parallel to BC by showing triangles on DE as base are equal and hence between same parallels. The proposition is biconditional (parallel <=> proportional cuts).

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. III. (Book VI) THEOR. (Angle bisector theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the angle of a triangle be divided into two equal angles by a straight line which also cuts the base; the segments of the base shall have the same ratio which the other sides of the triangle have to one another: and if the segments of the base have the same ratio which the other sides of the triangle have to one another, the straight line drawn from the vertex to the point of section divides the vertical angle into two equal angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forward: If AD bisects angle BAC, then BD:DC = BA:AC. Proof uses drawing through C a line parallel to AD meeting BA produced and shows corresponding triangles equal so AE = AC and then apply Prop. II to get the ratio. Converse: if BD:DC = BA:AC then joining AD implies AD bisects angle BAC by reversing the argument (show AE = AC and equal alternate/interior angles).

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. A. (Book VI) THEOR. (External angle bisector theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the outward angle of a triangle, made by producing one of its sides, be divided into two equal angles by a straight line which also cuts the base produced; the segments between the dividing line and the extremities of the base have the same ratio which the other sides of the triangle have to one another: and if the segments of the base produced have the same ratio which the other sides of the triangle have, the straight line drawn from the vertex to the point of section divides the outward angle of the triangle into two equal angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to Prop. III but for an external angle: forward direction shows BD:DC = BA:AC when AD bisects external angle CAE; converse deduces equal external angles from the given ratio by constructing parallels and applying previous proportionality results.

rubrics_metrics.name: PROP. IV. (Book VI) THEOR.
rubrics_metrics.description: The sides about the equal angles of equiangular triangles are proportionals; and those which are opposite to the equal angles are homologous sides, that is, are the antecedents or consequents of the ratios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let ABC and DCE be equiangular triangles with corresponding equal angles; then sides about equal angles are proportional and sides opposite equal angles are homologous. Proof places one triangle adjacent to the other and constructs parallels so corresponding sides are in parallel positions; uses earlier results about parallels and proportions to deduce side proportionality.
